verdict.rationale: The table texts set conditions for partaking that are self-directed and moral, but they do not lexically settle whether admission is governed by the universal body of believers, by a believer known to be walking with the Lord, or by membership in a bounded local assembly. In 1 Corinthians 11 the imperative dokimazeto heauton, let a person examine himself, aims the test at the self and the manner of partaking, anaxios, unworthily, an adverb. The next clause warns the one me diakrinon to soma, not discerning the body, but diakrino is attested across the canon in two senses, discern versus doubt or contend, and to soma can mean the eucharistic loaf or the corporate church, so the words do not rank the readings. 1 Corinthians 10:17 presses heis and pantes, one bread and all partake, toward inclusion, while 1 Corinthians 5:11 forbids even to eat with, synesthiein, a so-called brother in named scandal, which presumes a community that can identify and judge. The qualifiers about denominational affiliation and baptismal mode are post-canonical categories with no anchor lemma, so the scope of the table remains materially contested.

scripture.force: Whoever eats the bread or drinks the cup of the Lord unworthily, anaxios, an adverb of manner, becomes liable, enochos, with respect to the body and blood. anaxios is near a hapax, present only here and in a contested reading of verse 29, so its precise force cannot be triangulated from canon usage. The conditional clause hos an esthie e pine targets the mode of partaking, not the partaker's group membership.

dokimazeto de anthropos heauton is a present active imperative third singular directed reflexively at the self, let a person examine himself, and so eat. dokimazo carries a stable pan-epistolary sense of testing in order to approve, used of metals and of persons, as in 2Cor.13.5 examine yourselves. The qualification placed on the table is self-scrutiny, a test the individual applies to himself, not lexically an external admission check by an assembly.

ho gar esthion kai pinon krima heauto esthiei me diakrinon to soma. The participle diakrinon governs to soma. Two lexical underdeterminations stack here. First, diakrino is attested across the canon in roughly balanced senses, distinguish or discern as in Acts 15:9, versus doubt, waver, or contend as in Romans 4:20 and James 1:6, and the lexicon entry itself glosses it to judge or doubt. Second, to soma can denote the eucharistic loaf or the corporate church, the same word that in 1Cor.12.12 and 12.27 names the gathered body. Neither ambiguity is ranked by the words, and both bear directly on whether the table is bounded by a definite body.

The cup and the broken bread are named koinonia, fellowship or participation, of the blood and body of Christ. koinonia is used pan-epistolary for shared participation among those who belong to Christ, including the early breaking of bread in Acts 2:42. The term frames the table as a participation in Christ shared by his people, which can be read to extend to all who belong to him.

hoti heis artos, hen soma hoi polloi esmen, hoi gar pantes ek tou henos artou metechomen. One bread, one body the many are, for all partake, pantes metechomen, of the one bread. The lexical weight of heis and pantes presses toward a single shared participation of the many, supporting an inclusive reading of who shares the loaf. The same soma is linked by cross-reference to 1Cor.12.12, where the one body has many members, which keeps the corporate reading equally live.

The instruction me synesthiein, expressed with mede, not even to eat with, a so-called brother named in scandal sets a disciplinary boundary on table fellowship. synesthio, to eat together with, occurs only five times and carries the covenantal weight of shared meals, as in its Septuagint background and in the disputes over eating with sinners and with Gentiles. This grounds the proposition's exclusion of one under discipline, but it locates exclusion in named moral scandal, not in affiliation, and it presumes a community that can identify and judge such a one.

te koinonia, te klasei tou artou, the fellowship and the breaking of the bread, lists the early gathered believers continuing together in shared participation and bread. The narrative describes a single undivided company without any lexical marker of denominational sorting or admission test, which the inclusive reading takes as the baseline pattern, though the text names no admission policy and presumes those already added to their number.

ton de asthenounta te pistei proslambanesthe, me eis diakriseis dialogismon. Receive the one weak in the faith, but not for disputes over opinions. proslambano means to take to oneself, welcome, receive, and the imperative commands welcome and forbids making secondary opinion a basis for division, which supports receiving believers across differences.

ho theos gar auton proselabeto. God has received him. The ground for mutual reception is that God himself has received the other believer, removing one believer's standing to despise, exouthenein, or condemn another over disputed practice. The verb proslambano here matches the welcome imperative of verse 1.

su tis ei ho krinon allotrion oiketen. Who are you to judge the household servant of another. To his own master, idio kyrio, he stands or falls. The rhetorical question restrains one believer from judging another whom the Lord upholds, but it addresses internal mutual judgment over disputed practice, not the formal question of admission to the table.

complicating_texts.resolution: The command mede synesthiein, not even to eat with, a so-called brother in named scandal supplies the proposition's not-under-discipline exclusion, and its cross-reference to 1Cor.5.13, put away the evil one from among yourselves, implies that the community administering the table can identify and judge participants, which leans toward a bounded local table rather than an unqualified open one.

The referent of to soma in me diakrinon to soma is lexically undetermined between the eucharistic loaf and the corporate church, and diakrino itself is canonically polysemous between discern and doubt. No syntactic or apparatus datum in the store settles either, so whether discerning the body entails recognizing the bounds of a definite body remains open and bears on the open versus bounded reading.

The contrast between the cup of the Lord and the cup of demons shows the table marks a real allegiance boundary, but the boundary it draws is between Christ and idols, not between bodies of believers, so it neither confirms nor refutes the denominational clause of the proposition.

variants.note: Anchor verses are in 1 Corinthians, Romans, and Acts, all outside the 3 John ECM-published sample, so not_in_ecm_scope holds. The store lists no populated variant units for these refs. A known referential variant at 1Cor.11.29, whether tou kyriou is read after soma, does not alter the contested-scope verdict, since the ambiguity over the body is referential and lexical rather than text-critical.

competing_lens_verdicts.rationale: Reading soma in 1Cor.10.17 as the one body of all believers, koinonia as participation shared by all who belong to Christ, and proslambanesthe in Romans 14 as a command to receive any believer God has received, supports admitting any believer not in named scandal, irrespective of affiliation or baptismal mode. anaxios and dokimazeto place the test on the individual's manner and self-state, not on group membership.

Reading diakrino as discern and synesthiein in 1Cor.5.11 as a real exclusion implies the table admits believers known to be walking with the Lord and not in scandal, a middle position that fences by discernible moral and credal state rather than by membership. The Greek requires self-examination and excludes the scandalous but does not name how a stranger believer is assessed, so this reading is lexically possible but not compelled.

Reading me diakrinon to soma with soma as the gathered body, and the eat-not-with and put-away commands of 1Cor.5.11 and 5.13 as functions of a definite community that judges its own, implies the assembly administers and bounds its own table, so an unqualified regardless-of-affiliation admission is not lexically required. soma in 1Cor.12.12 and 12.27 names a definite body with members, which keeps this reading live.

hermeneutics.notes: The verdict turns on the polysemy of diakrino, on the referent of soma as loaf or corporate body, and on whether table admission is a self-applied test, a discernment of a believer's state, or a community-administered membership boundary. All three are exegetically live on the given Greek, which is why the proposition is graded disputed rather than affirmed or denied.

stem_audit.neutralized_form: What conditions, if any, does the New Testament place on a believer's admission to the Lord's table, and at what level, the individual partaker, the believer's discernible state, the local assembly, or the whole body of Christ, are those conditions applied?
stem_audit.notes: The original stem embeds a should plus a specific resolution toward an open table, and it uses the post-canonical categories denominational affiliation and baptismal mode, which have no anchor lemma in the store. The verdict was derived on the original stem, but it is recorded as disputed because the neutral question it presupposes is not lexically closed. No verdict change from the prior file. The 1Cor.5.11 anchor was corrected from esthio and adelphos to the lexically precise synesthio and mede, the actual eat-with-not-even construction, which sharpens but does not move the verdict.

lay_summary: The proposition says the Lord's table should be open to any believer walking with the Lord and not under discipline, regardless of denomination or how they were baptized. The Greek of the core texts pushes in more than one direction. In First Corinthians eleven the command is reflexive: let a person examine himself, dokimazeto heauton, and so eat. That verb means to test in order to approve, and it places the check on the partaker's own manner of eating, signaled by the adverb unworthily, anaxios, a word so rare it appears nowhere else to fix its sense. The next clause warns the one who eats without discerning the body, me diakrinon to soma. Here two separate ambiguities stack. The verb diakrino is used across the canon about evenly for two things, to discern or distinguish, and to doubt or waver, so the words alone do not tell us which is meant. And the word body, soma, can mean the bread on the table or the gathered church, the very word used elsewhere for the one body with many members. Neither ambiguity is settled by the grammar. Pulling toward openness, First Corinthians ten says one bread, one body, and all partake, pantes metechomen, and the early believers simply continued in the breaking of bread and fellowship, koinonia, with no admission test named. Romans fourteen reinforces this: receive the one weak in faith, proslambanesthe, because God has already received him. Pulling the other way, First Corinthians five says not even to eat with, synesthiein, a so-called brother in open scandal, and to put the evil one away, which presumes a community that can identify and judge who sits at the table. So the words clearly require self-examination and clearly exclude the unrepentant scandalous, which is exactly the not-under-discipline limit the proposition names. But the words do not rank the three live readings: a table open to all believers, a table for any believer discerned to be walking rightly, or a table bounded by a definite assembly. The terms denomination and baptismal mode have no word behind them here, since those categories arose later. That is why the question is genuinely contested at the level of the text itself.
